breaking.headline: Anthropic debuts on Nasdaq today as ANT after record $81B IPO
breaking.fact: Anthropic’s shares start trading on the Nasdaq today under the ticker ANT after pricing at $83 a share — above its $70–$78 range — in a record $81.3 billion offering upsized to 980 million shares; the deal was about six times oversubscribed and early indications pointed to a first trade well above the IPO price.

breaking.headline: Gold sinks to a 14-month low as December hike bets surge
breaking.fact: Gold fell nearly 3% on Wednesday to about $3,729 an ounce, its lowest in 14 months, as the dollar hit a 19-month high and traders priced a roughly 95% chance of a December Fed rate hike; it steadied near that level this morning.

breaking.headline: Moody’s cuts Nvidia’s outlook to stable after Huang’s exit
breaking.fact: Moody’s lowered Nvidia’s credit outlook to stable from positive on Wednesday, keeping its Aa1 rating but saying an upgrade is unlikely for 12 to 18 months, citing uncertainty over strategy and financial policy after Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation without a succession plan.

breaking.headline: Walmart beats and raises its outlook as shoppers keep spending
breaking.fact: Walmart reported third-quarter revenue of $188.8 billion, up 5.2%, and adjusted earnings of $0.65 a share, beating estimates, and raised full-year guidance to $2.84–$2.89 a share; U.S. comparable sales rose 2.9% and e-commerce grew 23%.

weekInBrief.headline: Dollar hits a 19-month high as hike bets build
weekInBrief.body: The dollar index pushed to about 103.9, its highest since April 2025, as traders priced a December Fed hike at roughly 95% and the euro slipped toward 1.097 — a tailwind for U.S. buyers of foreign assets and a headwind for multinationals’ overseas earnings.

weekInBrief.headline: Oil slides to its lowest since August on a big U.S. stock build
weekInBrief.body: WTI settled at $83.26 a barrel, down 3.2% and its lowest since August 26, while Brent settled at $91.95, after the EIA reported U.S. crude inventories rose 3.4 million barrels last week against forecasts of almost no change; both benchmarks are down roughly 20% in November.

weekInBrief.headline: Small caps flash a ‘death cross’ as the selloff broadens
weekInBrief.body: Small-cap stocks printed a classic death-cross chart pattern, confirming deep weakness in the Russell 2000, as the market’s slide spread beyond the AI names that led it — the S&P 500 has now fallen five sessions running.

weekInBrief.headline: Jobless claims edge up to 203,000, above forecasts
weekInBrief.body: Initial claims for unemployment benefits rose 1,000 to a seasonally adjusted 203,000 last week, above the 197,000 economists expected, while continuing claims jumped 70,000 to 1.763 million — a stable labor market, but with laid-off workers taking longer to find new jobs.

items.headline: Latest from the Strait
items.body: The week’s attacks on shipping escalated on Wednesday: a tanker was struck by a projectile in its engine room about six nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, in the evening, with its crew safe, a day after an ADNOC tanker was hit in the same area, leaving one seafarer missing and 11 injured. Iran launched drone attacks against American military facilities in Kuwait and Bahrain on Wednesday after U.S. strikes hit a Revolutionary Guards missile installation on Qeshm Island, overlooking the strait; U.S. Central Command said no American personnel were hurt. On oil, Washington widened the blockade on Wednesday to cover Iranian crude moved through ship-to-ship transfers — not just cargo loaded at Iranian ports — while CENTCOM says U.S.-escorted non-Iranian crude keeps flowing through the strait.

space.headline: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth
space.body: NASA’s Voyager 1, launched in 1977 and the most distant human-made object, reached one light-day from Earth — about 26 billion kilometers — on Wednesday, nearly 50 years into a mission that continues to study magnetic fields in interstellar space.

space.headline: NASA finds clues to ancient ice beyond Neptune
space.body: Twelve microscopic dust grains collected from Earth’s stratosphere by NASA’s ER-2 aircraft carry chemical traces of ancient water from the Kuiper Belt, the strongest evidence yet for a vast, isolated reservoir of heavy water beyond Neptune, published in Science Advances.

space.headline: Webb confirms a first-of-its-kind stellar merger
space.body: The James Webb Space Telescope clinched the first confirmed case of a sun-like star spiraling into and merging with a puffy supergiant — nicknamed Bao — on the outskirts of the Andromeda galaxy, with Webb observing just 47 days after the eruption peaked; the work is published in Nature.

space.headline: Quantum physics can now verify where a person is
space.body: NIST researchers ran the first complete demonstration of quantum position verification, using entangled photons and a loophole-free Bell test across two stations 195 meters apart in Boulder to prove a person’s location without trusting their device; practical use is still a decade or more away. Published in Nature.

apod.title: The Horsehead and Flame Nebulas
apod.credit: Mark E. Killion — NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day, November 19, 2026
apod.explanation: Today's image could have been a painting. But what do these colors mean? The brightest star, left of the center, is blue Alnitak (the Girdle): a triple star system best known for being the easternmost star in Orion's Belt. The instantly recognizable shape of a dark horse's head at the center is the aptly named Horsehead Nebula. It is about five light-years tall and lies approximately 1,500 light-years away. It is made of dust and gas that obscure the red glow behind it, which is caused by hydrogen gas being ionized by the bright star Sigma Orionis at the top. The orange nebula with dark filaments on the left is the Flame Nebula. Closer to the Horsehead, the blue reflection nebula NGC 2023 is actively forming stars. The data for this 'painting' were collected for almost six hours at the Utah Desert Remote Observatories, but the equipment was remotely controlled by the astrophotographer from his home, over 2,000 km away in Illinois.
